source.title: Double Trouble in Double Descent : Bias and Variance(s) in the Lazy Regime
source.authors: Stéphane d'Ascoli; Maria Refinetti; G. Biroli; Florent Krzakala

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and figures are flattened, but the document is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent using a random-features regression model and numerical deep-network experiments in a lazy-learning setting; these are conceptual tests rather than direct reproductions of the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-error sweeps over random-feature count and network width, a training-sample-size sweep, and decompositions of error variance. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows. Training is run to convergence, but the paper does not report a sweep over epochs.
record.test_reason: The study derives analytical test-error curves for random-features regression across feature counts, with decompositions, ensembling and regularization. It also runs width sweeps on a 5-layer network in the lazy regime. These results bear directly on whether the peak and the second descent occur and what drives them. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors find that in random-features regression the peak comes only from noise and initialization variances. Bias and sampling variance undergo a phase transition and then plateau, so the benefit of overparametrization is only variance reduction. Ensembling suppresses these variances, and at K→∞ error is flat past the threshold. Near the lazy regime the network results are qualitatively similar. Away from it, ensembled error rises past the threshold, possibly due to feature learning. They also show that the optimum can be underparametrized.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops an analytical bias-variance account for random-features regression and runs separate lazy-regime deep-network experiments; it does not reproduce the original study’s method. It uses a high-dimensional asymptotic analysis and random-feature ensembles.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior changes with regularization λ, ensemble size K, signal-to-noise ratio, dataset size relative to input dimension, and the lazy-regime scaling parameter α. The deep-network ensemble curve is roughly flat beyond the threshold at α = 100 but increases beyond it at α = 10.

fits_no_version.finding: In the lazy regime, bias and sampling variance stay constant past P=N. The whole second descent comes from shrinking initialization and noise variance, and it vanishes under infinite ensembling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of overparametrization beyond the interpolation threshold is solely variance reduction over random initialization; it is equivalent to ensembling, not a bias reduction.

record.problems: The analytical results use a heuristic, non-rigorous replica method. Deep-network experiments cover one binary task using only the first ten PCA components of CIFAR-10 and one five-layer fully-connected architecture. Many plotted results have no numerical values in the text; uncertainty is reported only for some simulations.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted. Figure 7 is retained as figure-only sample-size evidence because the paper gives no textual direction or numerical values for the changes.

untested.parts: The single-network (K=1) curve shape is figure-only and only partly described. Only one architecture and one task (binary 10-PCA CIFAR-10) are used.
Figure 7 sweeps N/D, but the text gives no direction of change near the threshold.
Multiple or triple peaks are not tested. It is not shown whether optimally tuned λ removes the peak: Fig 8 compares optimal λ only against infinite ensembling.

missing.what: Single-network (K=1) width sweep: the threshold is 'signalled by the peak' in test error at about 30 nodes per layer, and α=10 behaviour matches Geiger et al. The single-model peak is not recorded.
The location of optimal generalization moves to the underparametrized regime as K rises, SNR falls or N/D shrinks.
An optimally regularized single RF model versus an infinite ensemble: the infinite ensemble is always better. Whether the peak disappears under optimal λ is not stated.
Inverse power-law scaling: the divergence goes as (P/N−1)^-1, and initialization variance decays as (P/N)^-1.

record.verdict_notes: V1 rows were relinked: the RF model is a two-layer random-feature model, not a deep network, so RF rows now bear on V4 and V6. V1 evidence is limited to ensembled-network curves. The single-network curve needs extraction (see missing). V3 rows are all cannot_determine, so no V3 verdict is given. The analytical results rely on the non-rigorous replica method but are checked numerically.

versions.untested_parts: The deep-network experiment is limited to the stated binary CIFAR-10 setup and does not establish the pattern across other architectures or tasks.
No test-error-versus-epoch or training-time sweep is reported.

Figure 7 varies N/D at fixed P/D, but the text does not state the direction of the test-error change as sample count increases near the interpolation threshold; plotted values are not numerically reported.
The results concern random features and the paper's stated deep-network setup, not all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper analyzes noise and initialization variances and regularization smoothing. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether an optimally tuned regularizer makes the peak disappear.
The paper does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or show that this converts the second descent into an ordinary U-curve.

relationships.condition: Ensembles (K=20) of 5-layer FC nets on binary 10-PCA CIFAR-10, α=100 and α=10
relationships.reason: The ensembled curve is flat beyond the threshold near the lazy regime (r16). Away from it, error dips near the threshold and rises beyond it (r18). Any second descent depends on regime and ensembling.
relationships.display_finding: With 20 networks, error flattened beyond interpolation at α=100, whereas at α=10 it dipped near the threshold and then rose.

relationships.condition: RF model with ensembling (K≥2), larger regularization, or low SNR/small N/D
relationships.reason: Ensembling diminishes the peak, and at K→∞ error is constant past the threshold with no second descent (r12–r14). λ=0.1 removes the divergence (r2). From the text (Fig 12): with large K, low SNR or small N/D, the optimum lies in the underparametrized regime.
relationships.display_finding: Ensembling reduced the peak and made risk constant beyond interpolation as K approached infinity, while λ = 0.1 removed the divergence and large K, low SNR, or small N/D placed the optimum in the underparameterized regime.

source_check.reason: Split the conditions. The K→∞ curve in r14 has no post-threshold descent and challenges V4 in that setting. Finite K in r12–r13 attenuates the peak while retaining double descent. Removing a divergence through regularization does not itself establish loss of the second descent, and Appendix A.3's underparametrized optimum does not establish its absence either.

relationships.reason: The peak comes entirely from diverging noise and initialization variances (r3, r4); bias and sampling variance only kink (r5, r6). Regularization removes the divergence (r7, r8), and ensembling suppresses it as 1/K (r12–r14).
relationships.display_finding: Only noise and initialization variances diverged; regularization removed the divergence, ensembling suppressed it as 1/K, and bias and sampling variance merely kinked.
